<section class="chapter wrap" id="ch0"><div class="ch-head"><span class="plate">0</span><div><p class="eyebrow">Chapter 0 · All commands, in sequence</p><h2>Run from scratch</h2></div></div><div class="story"><span class="tag">The story so far</span><p>This chapter is the full path: from an empty computer to a trained model. You can use it on a new computer or to repair this one.</p><p>Do the cards from the top to the bottom. After each card, compare your screen with "What you must see". If it is different, stop and find the problem first.</p><p>You do not need to understand the model for this. Chapters 1 to 3 explain it.</p></div><div class="goals"><b>After this chapter you can</b><ul><li>Install the project without Docker.</li><li>Know which steps are done on your computer.</li><li>Run a test and a training.</li></ul></div><div class="cards"><article class="card solo" id="c0-1"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">0.1</span><h3>The full path on one page</h3><span class="slides">Status: 25 November 2026</span><label class="got" for="got-c0-1"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c0-1" data-got="c0-1"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Step</th><th>What you do</th><th>On your computer</th></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-2">0.2</a></td><td>Check the computer</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-3">0.3</a></td><td>Get the code and the repairs</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span>, but not saved in Git</td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-4">0.4</a></td><td>Make the environment (9.3 GB)</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-5">0.5</a></td><td>Install the Python packages</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-6">0.6</a></td><td>Build the fast code</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-7">0.7</a></td><td>Change three settings</td><td><span class="nope">Not done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-8">0.8</a></td><td>Get the checkpoints (0.9 GB)</td><td><span class="yes">Done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-9">0.9</a></td><td>Get the data (approximately 4 GB)</td><td><span class="nope">Not done</span></td></tr><tr><td><a href="#c0-10">0.10</a></td><td>Test, train and draw</td><td><span class="nope">Not done</span> with real data</td></tr></table></div><div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">On your computer, do only 0.7, 0.9 and 0.10. On a new computer, do all cards.</mark></p></div><figure class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 640 120" role="img" aria-label="Code, environment, build, settings, checkpoints and data, then run">

<article class="card" id="c0-2"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">0.2</span><h3>Check the computer</h3><span class="slides">New computer</span><label class="got" for="got-c0-2"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c0-2" data-got="c0-2"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><p>You need Linux, an NVIDIA graphics card, and 20 GB of free disk space.</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>nvidia-smi
df -h ~
free -h
conda --version
git --version</pre></div><p>If <code>conda</code> is missing, get <b>Miniforge</b> from its official page: <a href="https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge" target="_blank" rel="noopener">github.com/conda-forge/miniforge</a>.</p><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p>This project uses CUDA 11.3. It does not know graphics cards of the RTX 40 series or newer. Use a GTX 16, RTX 20 or RTX 30 card.</p></div><div class="box exam"><span class="tag">Security</span><p>Download only from the pages in this chapter. A checkpoint (<code>.pth</code>) from another website can contain a harmful program.</p></div><p class="oneline">Linux, NVIDIA card, 20 GB, conda.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>nvidia-smi:  GeForce GTX 1650
             driver 580.178.04
conda:       26.9.4
free disk:   140 GB</pre><figcaption>What you must see (your computer)</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c0-3"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">0.3</span><h3>Get the code and the repairs</h3><span class="slides">New computer</span><label class="got" for="got-c0-3"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c0-3" data-got="c0-3"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><p><b>A.</b> On your <b>old</b> computer, save the repairs in one small file. Copy this file to the home folder of the new computer.</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>cd ~/Workspace/Work_V/bevfusion
git diff 326653d -- mmdet3d &gt; ~/bevfusion-repairs.patch</pre></div><p><b>B.</b> On the <b>new</b> computer, get the code. Use the same version, then add the repairs.</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>mkdir -p ~/Workspace/Work_V
cd ~/Workspace/Work_V
git clone https://github.com/mit-han-lab/bevfusion.git
cd bevfusion
git switch -c my-work 326653d
git apply ~/bevfusion-repairs.patch
git status --short</pre></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">Key idea</span><p>The original code has errors on this version: it looks for parts that are not included. The repairs also decrease the memory. Thus you need them <b>before</b> the build.</p></div><div class="box note"><span class="tag">From our tests on your computer</span><p class="hand">The repair file operates</p><p>We made this file, applied it to a fresh copy of the code, and compared. All 7 files were identical.</p></div><p class="oneline">Same version of the code + your repair file.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>M mmdet3d/models/backbones/
     radar_encoder.py
M mmdet3d/models/vtransforms/base.py
M .../vtransforms/depth_lss.py
M .../vtransforms/lss.py
M .../feature_decorator.py
M .../spconv/spconv_ops.h
M .../spconv/src/indice_cuda.cu</pre><figcaption>What you must see: 7 files</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c0-4"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">0.4</span><h3>Make the environment</h3><span class="slides">New computer · 9.3 GB</span><label class="got" for="got-c0-4"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c0-4" data-got="c0-4"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><p>An <b>environment</b> is a separate box for programs. It does not change the other programs on your computer. Do the commands one at a time.</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda create -n bevfusion python=3.8 -y
conda activate bevfusion</pre></div><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda install pytorch==1.10.1 torchvision==0.11.2 cudatoolkit=11.3 -c pytorch -c conda-forge -y</pre></div><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda install mkl==2024.0.0 -c conda-forge -y</pre></div><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda install -c nvidia/label/cuda-11.3.1 cuda-toolkit -y</pre></div><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda install -c conda-forge gxx_linux-64=9 gcc_linux-64=9 -y</pre></div><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda install -c conda-forge openmpi=4.0.4 mpi4py=3.0.3 -y</pre></div><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Package</th><th>Function</th></tr><tr><td>pytorch, torchvision</td><td>Calculates the model.</td></tr><tr><td>mkl</td><td>Fast math. A newer version breaks PyTorch 1.10.</td></tr><tr><td>cuda-toolkit</td><td>Translates code for the graphics card.</td></tr><tr><td>gcc, gxx</td><td>Translates C++ code. Your system version is too new.</td></tr><tr><td>openmpi, mpi4py</td><td><code>torchpack</code> needs these.</td></tr></table></div><p>Check:</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>conda deactivate
conda activate bevfusion
python -c &quot;import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))&quot;</pre></div><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p><code>CondaVerificationError</code>: the download was damaged. Do <code>rm -rf ~/miniforge3/pkgs/pytorch-1.10.1*</code>, then <code>conda clean --tarballs --packages -y</code>, then install again.</p><p><code>iJIT_NotifyEvent</code>: you did not install <code>mkl==2024.0.0</code>.</p></div><p class="oneline">Six installs, then one check.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>1.10.1 11.3 True
NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650</pre><figcaption>What you must see</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>

<article class="card" id="c0-6"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">0.6</span><h3>Build the fast code</h3><span class="slides">New computer</span><label class="got" for="got-c0-6"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c0-6" data-got="c0-6"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><p>The parts in <code>mmdet3d/ops/</code> are C++ and CUDA. The computer must translate them one time. This takes some minutes.</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>export CUDA_HOME=$CONDA_PREFIX TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=&quot;7.5&quot; MAX_JOBS=2
python setup.py develop</pre></div><p>Check:</p><div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>python -c &quot;from mmdet3d.ops import Voxelization, bev_pool; print(&#x27;build OK&#x27;)&quot;</pre></div><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p><code>7.5</code> is for GTX 16 and RTX 20 cards. For an RTX 30 card write <code>8.6</code>.</p><p>If the build stops with <code>Killed</code>, the memory is full. Use <code>MAX_JOBS=1</code>.</p></div><p class="oneline">Build one time, then check.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>build OK</pre><figcaption>What you must see</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>

<section class="chapter wrap" id="ch1"><div class="ch-head"><span class="plate">1</span><div><p class="eyebrow">Chapter 1 · No code</p><h2>See the world</h2></div></div><div class="story"><span class="tag">The story so far</span><p>You join a team that builds a self-driving car. The car has six cameras and one laser on the roof.</p><p>Your job: the computer must look at this data and say "there is a car, 10 meters in front, and it moves".</p><p>This chapter explains the words that everybody in the project uses. You do not need any knowledge.</p></div><div class="goals"><b>After this chapter you can</b><ul><li>Say what a pixel, a point, and a voxel are.</li><li>Tell why one sensor is not sufficient.</li><li>Explain the map from above (BEV).</li></ul></div><div class="cards"><article class="card" id="c1-1"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.1</span><h3>The problem: what and where</h3><span class="slides">Demo video · frame 1</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-1"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-1" data-got="c1-1"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>A self-driving car must know two things about each object near it:</p>
<ul><li><b>What</b> is the object? A car, a person, a traffic cone.</li><li><b>Where</b> is the object? For example, 10 meters in front and 3 meters to the left.</li></ul>
<p>BEVFusion is a program that finds these two answers. It uses data from <b>sensors</b>. A sensor is a part that measures the world.</p>
<div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">BEVFusion reads 6 photos and one laser scan. It gives a list of 3D boxes. Each box has a type, a position, a size, a direction and a speed.</mark></p></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the picture</span><p>The left side shows the 6 photos. The black square shows the laser scan from above. Each colored box is an object that the program found. At the right, the program colored the road. The video plays at the right. Push it to make it larger.</p></div><p class="oneline">The program answers two questions: what is it, and where is it.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0" ><img src="data:image/gif;base64," alt="Six photos with boxes, a laser scan from above with boxes, and a colored road map"><figcaption>Authors' demo video · plays directly</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Front camera photo with orange boxes around cars"><figcaption>Front photo, larger · boxes around cars</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c1-2"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.2</span><h3>Camera and LiDAR</h3><span class="slides">Demo video · Paper Table IV</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-2"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-2" data-got="c1-2"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The <b class="cc">camera</b> makes a photo. A photo is a grid of small colored squares. One square is a <b>pixel</b>. The computer keeps each pixel as numbers.</p>
<p>The <b class="ll">LiDAR</b> is a laser on the roof. It sends light and measures the time until the light comes back. A long time means that the object is far away. Each measurement gives one <b>point</b>. Many points together are a <b>point cloud</b>.</p>
<div class="play"><b class="ph2">Try it: which sensor helps more?</b><div class="jsonly"><div class="row" id="cond"></div><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u id="bc" style="background:var(--amber)"></u></i><span id="tc"></span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u id="bl" style="background:var(--blue)"></u></i><span id="tl"></span></div><p class="out" id="condt" aria-live="polite"></p></div><div class="nojs tabs "><label><input type="radio" name="ns" checked><span>Clear day</span></label><div class="tp"><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u style="background: var(--amber); width: 90%;"></u></i><span>much</span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u style="background: var(--blue); width: 70%;"></u></i><span>much</span></div><p class="out">The camera shows what the objects are. The LiDAR shows where they are.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="ns"><span>Dark night</span></label><div class="tp"><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u style="background: var(--amber); width: 25%;"></u></i><span>small</span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u style="background: var(--blue); width: 70%;"></u></i><span>much</span></div><p class="out">The camera has little light. The LiDAR makes its own light.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="ns"><span>Read a traffic sign</span></label><div class="tp"><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u style="background: var(--amber); width: 90%;"></u></i><span>much</span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u style="background: var(--blue); width: 10%;"></u></i><span>small</span></div><p class="out">The LiDAR sees no color and no text. The camera does.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="ns"><span>Measure distance</span></label><div class="tp"><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u style="background: var(--amber); width: 25%;"></u></i><span>small</span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u style="background: var(--blue); width: 95%;"></u></i><span>much</span></div><p class="out">The LiDAR measures distance directly. The camera must estimate it.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="ns"><span>Far object</span></label><div class="tp"><div class="bars"><span class="cc">Camera</span><i><u style="background: var(--amber); width: 65%;"></u></i><span>medium</span><span class="ll">LiDAR</span><i><u style="background: var(--blue); width: 25%;"></u></i><span>small</span></div><p class="out">Few laser points touch a far object. The photo still shows it.</p></div></div><p class="small">The bars show the idea only. They are not measurements.</p></div>
<div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>The camera is like your eyes. The LiDAR is like a person who touches everything with a long stick. Your eyes see colors. The stick measures distance, also in the dark.</p></div><div class="wn"><div class="ok"><b class="h">Camera: strong when</b><ul><li>it must see color, text or a traffic light</li><li>the object is far away and has few laser points</li></ul></div><div class="no"><b class="h">Camera: weak when</b><ul><li>it is dark</li><li>it must measure distance exactly</li></ul></div></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>The camera is strong where the LiDAR is weak, and the LiDAR is strong where the camera is weak. Thus the program uses the two together. This is <b>fusion</b>. Table IV of the paper shows the result: at night the LiDAR-only model gets 35.4 and BEVFusion gets 42.8 (mAP).</p></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c1-6">1.6</a> why older programs lost data when they joined the sensors</li><li><a href="#c2-6">2.6</a> what the score mAP means</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">Camera = what it looks like. LiDAR = how far it is. Fusion = use both.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Six camera photos with boxes"><figcaption>Six photos · all directions</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Laser points from above in white on black"><figcaption>LiDAR points · seen from above</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Table of scores in sun, rain, day and night"><figcaption>Paper Table IV · sun, rain, night</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c1-3"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.3</span><h3>Voxels: small boxes in space</h3><span class="slides">configs/nuscenes/default.yaml</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-3"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-3" data-got="c1-3"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>A pixel is a small square in a flat photo. A <b>voxel</b> is a small box in space.</p>
<p>The points of the LiDAR are not in a regular pattern. A computer works better with a regular grid. Thus the program divides the space into boxes and puts each point into its box.</p>

<div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>Think of a block-building game. The world is made of blocks of the same size. Each block is empty or has something in it.</p></div><div class="wn"><div class="ok"><b class="h">Small boxes: good</b><ul><li>they keep more detail</li><li>you see a thin object, for example a pole</li></ul></div><div class="no"><b class="h">Small boxes: bad</b><ul><li>they use more memory</li><li>your graphics card has only 4 GB</li></ul></div></div><div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>The small model looks at a space of 102.4 m × 102.4 m. One box is 0.1 m wide.</p><ol class="steps"><li>Boxes in one direction: <span class="m">102.4 / 0.1 = 1024</span>.</li><li>Boxes in all directions, with 41 layers: <span class="m">1024 × 1024 × 41 = 42,991,616</span>.</li><li>The recipe keeps a maximum of 90,000 boxes in training: <span class="m">90,000 / 42,991,616 = 0.2 %</span>.</li></ol><p class="inwords">Almost all boxes are empty. The program calculates only the full ones. This is a <b>sparse</b> calculation.</p></div><p class="oneline">A voxel is a small box in space. Most of them are empty, and the program ignores those.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>point_cloud_range: [-51.2, -51.2, -5.0,
                     51.2,  51.2,  3.0]
voxel_size: [0.1, 0.1, 0.2]
image_size: [256, 704]</pre><figcaption>configs/nuscenes/default.yaml · the space and the box</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>voxelize:
  max_num_points: 10
  max_voxels: [90000, 120000]
  # training: 90000, test: 120000</pre><figcaption>lidar/voxelnet.yaml · the maximum</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c1-4"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.4</span><h3>The map from above (BEV)</h3><span class="slides">Paper Figure 2</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-4"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-4" data-got="c1-4"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>A photo looks forward. A point cloud has three directions. You cannot put one on the other directly.</p>
<p>The solution is the main idea of this project. The program changes the two into the same kind of map. The map shows the world from above. This is <b class="mm">bird's-eye view</b>, or <b>BEV</b>.</p>
<div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">Photos become a map from above. LiDAR points become a map from above. The squares of the two maps have the same size. Thus the program can put one map on the other.</mark></p></div><figure class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" role="img" aria-label="Photos and LiDAR points each become a map from above, then the program puts the two maps together and finds objects">
<defs><marker id="ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
<rect class="bx amber" x="4" y="20" width="110" height="56" rx="6"/><rect class="bx blue" x="4" y="134" width="110" height="56" rx="6"/><rect class="bx amber" x="212" y="20" width="110" height="56" rx="6"/><rect class="bx blue" x="212" y="134" width="110" height="56" rx="6"/><rect class="bx green" x="400" y="77" width="100" height="56" rx="6"/><rect class="bx" x="560" y="77" width="76" height="56" rx="6"/>
<g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><path d="M114 48H210" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><path d="M114 162H210" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><path d="M322 48L398 92" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><path d="M322 162L398 118" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><path d="M500 105H558" marker-end="url(#ar)"/></g>
<g text-anchor="middle"><text x="59" y="53">6 photos</text><text x="59" y="167">LiDAR points</text><text x="267" y="53">camera map</text><text x="267" y="167">LiDAR map</text><text x="450" y="110">one map</text><text x="598" y="110">objects</text><text class="s" x="162" y="40">estimate depth</text><text class="s" x="162" y="154">make voxels</text><text class="s" x="384" y="60">put together</text></g></svg><figcaption>The two lines become one line. The paper shows the same thing in Figure 2.</figcaption></figure><div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>The large model looks from −54 m to +54 m. One square of its final map is 0.6 m wide.</p><ol class="steps"><li>Width of the area: <span class="m">54 + 54 = 108 m</span>.</li><li>Squares in one direction: <span class="m">108 / 0.6 = 180</span>.</li></ol><p class="inwords">The map has 180 × 180 squares. A car is approximately 4.5 m long, thus it covers 7 or 8 squares.</p></div><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>You have a photo of a room and a list of distances. You cannot add them. But you can draw two floor plans of the room, one from each. Then you put one floor plan on the other.</p></div><p class="oneline">Both sensors make the same kind of map from above. Then joining them is easy.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Diagram of BEVFusion: camera line and LiDAR line become BEV features and are joined"><figcaption>Paper Figure 2 · the full system</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Laser points from above"><figcaption>A view from above</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c1-5"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.5</span><h3>How a photo becomes a map</h3><span class="slides">Paper Figure 3a · vtransforms/base.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-5"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-5" data-got="c1-5"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>One pixel gives a direction. It does not give the distance. Thus the program tries <b>118 distances</b> for each part of the photo, from 1 m to 59.5 m. It gives a score to each distance. A high score means that the distance is probably correct.</p>

The point is below the road. This is not possible on a flat road. It is outside the map, thus the program ignores it.</p></div></div><p class="small">This is one real part of the front photo, a small distance below the center. At this step the map has 360 × 360 squares of 0.3 m. The next step makes it 180 × 180 (card 1.4).</p></div>
<p>At 10 m, the line touches the road. Thus 10 m is probably correct. At 40 m, the point is below the road, and that is not possible. The program learns this from examples.</p>
<div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>One part of a photo has the feature value 10. The program gives these scores to three distances: 0.1, 0.7, 0.2.</p><ol class="steps"><li>Near: <span class="m">0.1 × 10 = 1</span></li><li>Middle: <span class="m">0.7 × 10 = 7</span></li><li>Far: <span class="m">0.2 × 10 = 2</span></li></ol><p class="inwords">The program puts most of the value (7) at the middle distance. The scores always add up to 1.</p></div><div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example: the number of points</span><p>How many 3D points do the photos make?</p><ol class="steps"><li>6 cameras × 118 distances = <span class="m">708</span></li><li>One small photo map has 32 × 88 parts = <span class="m">2,816</span></li><li>Together: <span class="m">708 × 2,816 = 1,993,728</span></li></ol><p class="inwords">Almost 2 million points for each example. The paper says the same: "around 2 million points". This is why this step needs much memory.</p></div><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p>If the program gives a high score to the wrong distance, the object appears at the wrong place in the map. This is the most usual camera error.</p></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c3-2">3.2</a> the camera side of the model</li><li><a href="#c5-1">5.1</a> the low memory setting makes this step smaller</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">One pixel is a direction. The program scores 118 distances and puts the feature at the probable ones.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Camera with three lines; each line has dots with scores"><figcaption>Paper Figure 3a · scores along each line</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>depth = x[:, : self.D].softmax(dim=1)
x = depth.unsqueeze(1) * x[
  :, self.D : (self.D + self.C)
].unsqueeze(2)</pre><figcaption>depth_lss.py:97-98 · score × feature</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c1-6"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">1.6</span><h3>Why older programs lost data</h3><span class="slides">Paper Figure 1</span><label class="got" for="got-c1-6"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c1-6" data-got="c1-6"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>Before BEVFusion, people joined the sensors in two other ways. Each way loses something.</p>
<div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Way</th><th>What it does</th><th>What it loses</th></tr><tr><td>To the camera</td><td>Draws the LiDAR points on the photo</td><td><b>Geometry.</b> Two points near each other in the photo can be far from each other in the world.</td></tr><tr><td>To the LiDAR</td><td>Gives each laser point the color or feature of one pixel</td><td><b>Meaning.</b> Only approximately 5 % of the camera features get a laser point. The program does not use the others.</td></tr><tr><td>To the map (BEVFusion)</td><td>Changes each sensor into a map from above</td><td>It keeps the two. But it must estimate the distance of each pixel.</td></tr></table></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the figure</span><p>Look at (a): the white circles show points that are near each other in the photo, but not in the world. Look at (b): the box shows a part of the street with no laser points. Look at (c): the two maps that BEVFusion makes.</p></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>The title of the paper says "unified bird's-eye view". The authors do not say that one sensor is the main sensor. The two sensors meet in a neutral place: the map.</p></div><p class="oneline">Photo loses distance, points lose meaning, the map from above keeps both.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Three panels: to camera, to LiDAR, and shared BEV"><figcaption>Paper Figure 1 · three ways to join</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
</div><div class="quiz" id="quiz1"><div class="quiz-h"><h3>Checkpoint 1: See the world</h3><span class="score"></span></div><div class="q" data-a="b"><p>It is dark and a person is in front of the car. <section class="chapter wrap" id="ch2"><div class="ch-head"><span class="plate">2</span><div><p class="eyebrow">Chapter 2 · No code</p><h2>How a program learns</h2></div></div><div class="story"><span class="tag">The story so far</span><p>Nobody can write a rule for each car, each color and each angle.</p><p>Thus we show the computer many examples with the correct answer. The computer finds the rules.</p><p>This is machine learning. This chapter gives you the six ideas that you need before you train a model.</p></div><div class="goals"><b>After this chapter you can</b><ul><li>Explain parameter, loss, step and epoch.</li><li>Say what a checkpoint is.</li><li>Read the two scores mAP and NDS.</li></ul></div><div class="cards"><article class="card solo" id="c2-1"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.1</span><h3>Models and parameters</h3><span class="slides">Counted on your computer</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-1"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-1" data-got="c2-1"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The program that learns is a <b>neural network</b>. We also call it a <b>model</b>.</p>
<p>The model contains many numbers. One such number is a <b>parameter</b>. The large camera and LiDAR model has <b>39.8 million</b> parameters.</p>
<p>The model multiplies and adds the input with its parameters, many times. The last result is the answer. A <b>feature</b> is a number in the middle that describes something. For example, one feature can mean "this looks like a wheel".</p>
<div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>A music mixer has many knobs. Each knob changes the sound a little. The model has 39.8 million knobs. <b>To train means to turn the knobs to the correct position.</b></p></div><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Part of the model</th><th>Parameters</th></tr><tr><td>Find photo features (Swin-T)</td><td>27.5 million</td></tr><tr><td>Look at a larger area</td><td>4.6 million</td></tr><tr><td>LiDAR network</td><td>2.7 million</td></tr><tr><td>Join photo features</td><td>1.6 million</td></tr><tr><td>Photo to map</td><td>1.6 million</td></tr><tr><td>Find objects</td><td>1.0 million</td></tr><tr><td>Put the maps together</td><td>0.8 million</td></tr></table></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c3-1">3.1</a> all the parts, and what each one does</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">A model is a large set of numbers. Training changes these numbers.</p></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c2-2"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.2</span><h3>Loss: how bad is the answer?</h3><span class="slides">Training test, 24 November 2026</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-2"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-2" data-got="c2-2"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>We give the model an example. The model gives an answer. We compare the answer with the correct answer. The result is one number, the <b>loss</b>.</p>
<div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">A large loss means a bad answer. A small loss means a good answer. In training, the loss must go down.</mark></p></div><div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>The correct box is at 10.0 m. The model says 12.5 m.</p><ol class="steps"><li>Difference: <span class="m">12.5 − 10.0 = 2.5</span></li><li>This part of the recipe has the weight 0.25: <span class="m">2.5 × 0.25 = 0.625</span></li></ol><p class="inwords">This is the idea of the L1 loss for boxes. The full loss adds the parts for position, size, direction, speed and type.</p></div><div class="box note"><span class="tag">From our tests on your computer</span><p class="hand">Loss: 484 → 3.9 in 120 steps</p><p>We trained <code>voxelnet.yaml</code> with artificial examples. The figure shows only that training operates. It does not show that the model is good.</p></div><p class="oneline">Loss is one number that tells how bad the answer is. Training makes it smaller.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="diagram side"><svg id="loss" viewBox="0 0 600 250" role="img" aria-label="Loss decreases from 484 to about 4 in 120 steps"><path <article class="card solo" id="c2-3"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.3</span><h3>One step, and the learning rate</h3><span class="slides">tools/train.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-3"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-3" data-got="c2-3"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The computer finds out how each parameter changes the loss. This information is the <b>gradient</b>. Then it changes each parameter by a small quantity, in the direction that decreases the loss. This is one <b>step</b>.</p>
<p>The <b>learning rate</b> (<code>lr</code>) tells how large the change is.</p>
<div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>A parameter is 3.0. The gradient is 2. The learning rate is 0.1.</p><ol class="steps"><li>Change: <span class="m">0.1 × 2 = 0.2</span></li><li>New parameter: <span class="m">3.0 − 0.2 = 2.8</span></li></ol><p class="inwords">Old number minus learning rate times gradient. The optimizer of this project does more than this, but the idea is the same.</p></div><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>You stand on a hill in fog. You want to go to the valley. You feel with your foot where the ground goes down, and you make one step. The learning rate is the length of your step.</p></div><div class="wn"><div class="ok"><b class="h">A good learning rate</b><ul><li>the loss goes down slowly and regularly</li></ul></div><div class="no"><b class="h">A bad learning rate</b><ul><li>lr is too large: the loss jumps or becomes <code>nan</code></li><li>lr is too small: the loss almost does not move</li></ul></div></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c7-1">7.1</a> change the learning rate with one line</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">One step = small change of all parameters. The learning rate is the size of the change.</p></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c2-4"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.4</span><h3>Epoch, batch and checkpoint</h3><span class="slides">configs/default.yaml</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-4"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-4" data-got="c2-4"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Word</th><th>Meaning</th><th>In this project</th></tr><tr><td><b>Batch</b></td><td>The examples in one step</td><td><code>samples_per_gpu</code>. Use 1 on your card.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Epoch</b></td><td>One pass through all the examples</td><td><code>max_epochs</code>. The LiDAR recipe uses 20.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Checkpoint</b></td><td>A file with the saved parameters</td><td>It ends with <code>.pth</code>.</td></tr></table></div><p>The program saves a checkpoint after each epoch. You can stop, and continue later from the checkpoint.</p><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the recipe</span><p><code>interval: 1</code> means: save after each epoch. <code>max_keep_ckpts: 1</code> means: keep only the newest file. The older ones are deleted.</p></div><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>An epoch is reading the full book one time. A batch is the number of pages that you read before you think. A checkpoint is a saved game.</p></div><p class="oneline">Batch = examples in one step. Epoch = one full pass. Checkpoint = saved game.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>checkpoint_config:
  interval: 1
  max_keep_ckpts: 1

resume_from: null
max_epochs: 20</pre><figcaption>configs/default.yaml · saving</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c2-5"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.5</span><h3>Training examples and test examples</h3><span class="slides">configs/nuscenes/default.yaml</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-5"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-5" data-got="c2-5"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>A student who learns the answers by heart gets a good result only with the same questions. A model can do the same. This is <b>overfitting</b>.</p>
<p>Thus the data has two parts. The model learns from the <b>training</b> part. We test it with the <b>validation</b> part, which it did not see.</p>
<p>There is a second help. The program changes each training example a little. It can turn it, mirror it, make it larger, or add objects. This is <b>augmentation</b>.</p>
<div class="wn"><div class="ok"><b class="h">Good sign</b><ul><li>loss goes down and the test score goes up</li></ul></div><div class="no"><b class="h">Bad sign</b><ul><li>loss goes down but the test score goes down: the model learns by heart</li></ul></div></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>A low loss is not the goal. A good score on new examples is the goal.</p></div><p class="oneline">Never judge a model with the examples that it learned from.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>augment3d:
  scale: [0.9, 1.1]
  rotate: [-0.78539816, 0.78539816]
  translate: 0.5
  # larger or smaller, turn, move</pre><figcaption>configs/nuscenes/default.yaml · small changes</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c2-6"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">2.6</span><h3>The scores: mAP and NDS</h3><span class="slides">Paper Table I · nuScenes</span><label class="got" for="got-c2-6"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c2-6" data-got="c2-6"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The test gives two scores. The two go from 0 (bad) to 1 (perfect). The paper multiplies them by 100.</p>
<ul><li><b>mAP</b> tells how many objects the model finds correctly. The center of the box must be near the correct center. nuScenes uses the limits 0.5 m, 1 m, 2 m and 4 m.</li><li><b>NDS</b> also includes the errors of position, size, direction, speed and attribute (for example "parked").</li></ul>
<div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Formula</span><p class="m" style="white-space:normal">NDS = (5 × mAP + sum of (1 − error) for the 5 errors) / 10</p><p class="inwords">mAP gives one half of the score. The five errors give the other half. An error larger than 1 counts as 1.</p><p>Example: mAP = 0.60. The errors are 0.30, 0.25, 0.30, 0.25 and 0.20.</p><ol class="steps"><li>1 − error: <span class="m">0.70 + 0.75 + 0.70 + 0.75 + 0.80 = 3.70</span></li><li>5 × mAP: <span class="m">5 × 0.60 = 3.00</span></li><li>NDS: <span class="m">(3.00 + 3.70) / 10 = 0.67</span></li></ol></div><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Model in the paper (validation)</th><th>mAP</th><th>NDS</th></tr><tr><td>CenterPoint, LiDAR only</td><td>59.6</td><td>66.8</td></tr><tr><td>TransFusion, camera and LiDAR</td><td>67.5</td><td>71.3</td></tr><tr><td><b>BEVFusion, camera and LiDAR</b></td><td><b>68.5</b></td><td><b>71.4</b></td></tr></table></div><div class="box note"><span class="tag">From our tests on your computer</span><p class="hand">Our NDS was 0.063</p><p>This was on artificial data after a very short training. The number has no meaning. You get a real score after you download nuScenes.</p></div><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p>The mini dataset is very small. Your scores on mini cannot be compared with the scores of the paper.</p></div><p class="oneline">mAP = found correctly. NDS = found correctly, and the box is good.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Table of detection scores with BEVFusion in the last row"><figcaption>Paper Table I · all scores</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Three line charts that compare BEVFusion with other models"><figcaption>Paper Figure 4 · size, distance, few beams</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
</div><div class="quiz" id="quiz2"><div class="quiz-h"><h3>Checkpoint 2: How a program learns</h3><span class="score"></span></div><div class="q" data-a="b"><p>The loss goes from 500 to 5. Is this good?</p><div class="opts jsonly"><button type="button" data-k="a">Yes, and no other test is necessary</button><button type="button" data-k="b">Yes, but you must also test with new examples</button><button type="button" data-k="c">No</button></div><p class="why" hidden>The answers are nearer to the correct answers. But a model can learn examples by heart.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q8"> <span>Yes, and no other test is necessary</span></label><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q8"> <span>Yes, but you must also test with new examples</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q8"> <span>No</span></label><p class="why2">The answers are nearer to the correct answers. But a model can learn examples by heart.</p></div></div><div class="q" data-a="c"><p>What is in a <code>.pth</code> file?</p><div class="opts jsonly"><button type="button" data-k="a">Photos</button><button type="button" data-k="b">The recipe</button><button type="button" data-k="c">The saved parameters</button></div><p class="why" hidden>It is a checkpoint: the saved numbers of the model.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q9"> <span>Photos</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q9"> <span>The recipe</span></label><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q9"> <span>The saved parameters</span></label><p class="why2">It is a checkpoint: the saved numbers of the model.</p></div></div><div class="q" data-a="a"><p>A parameter is 5.0, the gradient is 10, and lr is 0.01. What is the new parameter?</p><div class="opts jsonly"><button type="button" data-k="a">4.9</button><button type="button" data-k="b">4.0</button><button type="button" data-k="c">5.1</button></div><p class="why" hidden>5.0 − 0.01 × 10 = 5.0 − 0.1 = 4.9.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q10"> <span>4.9</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q10"> <span>4.0</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q10"> <span>5.1</span></label><p class="why2">5.0 − 0.01 × 10 = 5.0 − 0.1 = 4.9.</p></div></div><div class="q" data-a="b"><p>Which score includes the speed of the objects?</p><div class="opts jsonly"><button type="button" data-k="a">mAP</button><button type="button" data-k="b">NDS</button><button type="button" data-k="c">Loss only</button></div><p class="why" hidden>NDS includes the errors of position, size, direction, speed and attribute.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q11"> <span>mAP</span></label><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q11"> <span>NDS</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q11"> <span>Loss only</span></label><p class="why2">NDS includes the errors of position, size, direction, speed and attribute.</p></div></div></div></section>
<section class="chapter wrap" id="ch3"><div class="ch-head"><span class="plate">3</span><div><p class="eyebrow">Chapter 3 · First look at code</p><h2>The full model</h2></div></div><div class="story"><span class="tag">The story so far</span><p>You know the sensors, the voxels and the map from above. You also know how a program learns.</p><p>Now you put it together. The model is a line of stations, like a factory.</p><p>Read the code at the right side slowly. You do not need to understand each word. Find the names that you know.</p></div><div class="goals"><b>After this chapter you can</b><ul><li>Name the stations in the correct sequence.</li><li>Say which station makes which map.</li><li>Find the line of code that joins the two maps.</li></ul></div><div class="cards"><article class="card" id="c3-1"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.1</span><h3>The line of stations</h3><span class="slides">Paper Figure 2</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-1"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-1" data-got="c3-1"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>Data goes from the top to the bottom. Push a station to see its function.</p>
<div class="play"><div class="jsonly"><div class="lanes" id="lanes"></div><div id="stn" aria-live="polite"></div></div><div class="nojs tabs "><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Camera: 6 photos</span></label><div class="tp"><b>6 photos</b><p>The six cameras look in all directions. The program makes each photo 704 pixels wide and 256 pixels high.</p><p>Where: <code>datasets/</code>. Parameters: 0.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>LiDAR: LiDAR points</span></label><div class="tp"><b>LiDAR points</b><p>Each point has five numbers: three for position, one for brightness, one for time.</p><p>Where: <code>datasets/</code>. Parameters: 0.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Camera: Find photo features</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Find photo features</b><p>A network with the name Swin-T looks for edges, shapes and objects in each photo.</p><p>Where: <code>Swin-T comes from the mmdet library</code>. Parameters: 27.5 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>LiDAR: Make voxels</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Make voxels</b><p>The program puts the points into boxes.</p><p>Where: <code>mmdet3d/ops/voxel/</code>. Parameters: 0.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Camera: Join photo features</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Join photo features</b><p>This part joins features of small and large objects.</p><p>Where: <code>models/necks/generalized_lss.py</code>. Parameters: 1.6 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>LiDAR: LiDAR network</span></label><div class="tp"><b>LiDAR network</b><p>A sparse network looks at the boxes that contain points. Its output is the LiDAR map.</p><p>Where: <code>models/backbones/sparse_encoder.py</code>. Parameters: 2.7 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt" checked><span>Camera: Photo to map</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Photo to map</b><p>This part estimates the distance and puts the features into the camera map. See card 1.5.</p><p>Where: <code>models/vtransforms/depth_lss.py</code>. Parameters: 1.6 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Put the maps together</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Put the maps together</b><p>The program puts one map on the other. Then one small network mixes them. Each map has 180 × 180 squares.</p><p>Where: <code>models/fusers/conv.py</code>. Parameters: 0.8 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Look at a larger area</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Look at a larger area</b><p>A car is larger than one square. This part looks at many squares together.</p><p>Where: <code>models/backbones/second.py</code>. Parameters: 4.6 million.</p></div><label><input type="radio" name="nt"><span>Find objects</span></label><div class="tp"><b>Find objects</b><p>The head gives 200 boxes. Each box has a position, a size, a direction, a speed and a score. A low score means that the model is not sure.</p><p>Where: <code>models/heads/bbox/transfusion.py</code>. Parameters: 1.0 million.</p></div></div></div>
<div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">Camera side: photos → features → map. LiDAR side: points → voxels → map. Then: put together → look at a larger area → find objects.</mark></p></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c4-2">4.2</a> the file of each station</li><li><a href="#c4-5">4.5</a> the same line, in the code</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">Two lines make two maps. The maps become one. The head finds the objects.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Diagram of the full BEVFusion system"><figcaption>Paper Figure 2 · compare with the stations</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c3-2"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.2</span><h3>The camera side</h3><span class="slides">vtransforms/base.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-2"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-2" data-got="c3-2"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<ol><li><b>Find photo features.</b> The network Swin-T looks for edges, shapes and objects. This is the <b>backbone</b>.</li><li><b>Join photo features.</b> The <b>neck</b> joins the features of small and large objects.</li><li><b>Photo to map.</b> It scores 118 distances for each part (card 1.5).</li><li><b>Pool.</b> It adds all values that fall into the same square of the map.</li></ol>
<div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the code</span><p>Each value has a place in the world. Line 163 calculates which square it is. Lines 174 to 181 delete the values that are outside of the map. Line 185 adds the values in each square.</p></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>The fast pooling is a main result of the paper. The old method needed more than 500 ms on a large card. The new method needs 12 ms. This is approximately 40 times faster.</p></div><div class="box note"><span class="tag">From our tests on your computer</span><p class="hand">BEVFUSION_LOW_MEM=1</p><p>Pooling is a sum. Thus it can add one camera at a time and get the same result with less memory. This setting makes the camera models fit on your 4 GB card. We compared the results: the difference is less than 0.00001.</p></div><p class="oneline">Backbone finds, neck joins, transform gives distance, pool adds into squares.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre># which square?
geom_feats = ((geom_feats
   - (self.bx - self.dx / 2.0))
   / self.dx).long()
...
# add all values in one square
x = bev_pool(x, geom_feats, B,
   self.nx[2], self.nx[0], self.nx[1])</pre><figcaption>vtransforms/base.py:163, 185</figcaption></figure><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Figure of pooling methods and speed"><figcaption>Paper Figure 3 · fast pooling</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c3-3"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.3</span><h3>The LiDAR side</h3><span class="slides">bevfusion.py · sparse_encoder.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-3"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-3" data-got="c3-3"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<ol><li><b>Make voxels.</b> Each point goes into its box. If a box has more than one point, the program uses the mean.</li><li><b>Sparse network.</b> It looks at the full boxes and their neighbors. It makes the grid 8 times smaller in two directions.</li><li><b>Flatten.</b> It puts the layers of the grid together. The result is the LiDAR map.</li></ol>
<div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><p>The small model has 1024 boxes in one direction.</p><ol class="steps"><li>8 times smaller: <span class="m">1024 / 8 = 128</span> squares</li><li>Width of one square: <span class="m">0.1 m × 8 = 0.8 m</span></li></ol><p class="inwords">The small model makes a map of 128 × 128 squares. One square is 0.8 m wide.</p></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the code</span><p>Lines 192 to 194: add the points of one box, then divide by their number. That is the mean.</p></div><div class="box note"><span class="tag">From our tests on your computer</span><p class="hand">We saved 0.95 GB here</p><p>The sparse code kept memory for boxes with 4096 neighbors. This model does not use more than 256. We changed the value and built it again.</p></div><p class="oneline">Points → boxes → sparse network → flat map.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>feats = feats.sum(
    dim=1, keepdim=False
) / sizes.type_as(feats).view(-1, 1)</pre><figcaption>bevfusion.py:192-194 · the mean</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>N, C, H, W, D = spatial_features.shape
# C*D: put the layers together
spatial_features = (
  spatial_features.view(N, C * D, H, W))</pre><figcaption>sparse_encoder.py:128-130 · flatten</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c3-4"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.4</span><h3>Put the maps together</h3><span class="slides">fusers/conv.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-4"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-4" data-got="c3-4"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>This is the "fusion" in BEVFusion. It is the smallest file of all.</p>
<p>The camera map has 80 features for each square. The LiDAR map has 256. The program puts them one behind the other. Then one small network mixes them.</p>
<div class="box formula"><span class="tag">Worked example</span><ol class="steps"><li>Put together: <span class="m">80 + 256 = 336</span> features in each square.</li><li>The network looks at 3 × 3 squares and makes 256 new features.</li><li>Parameters: <span class="m">336 × 256 × 3 × 3 = 774,144</span>.</li></ol><p class="inwords">Approximately 0.8 million parameters. This agrees with the table in card 2.1.</p></div><div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need"><code>torch.cat</code> puts the maps together. The network after it mixes them.</mark></p></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>Why is a network necessary after <code>torch.cat</code>? The distance of the camera is an estimate. Thus an object in the camera map can be a little away from its place in the LiDAR map. The network looks at the neighbor squares and corrects this.</p></div><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>Two people draw the same city on transparent paper. One knows the colors, one knows the distances. You put the papers one on the other, and a third person draws the final map.</p></div><p class="oneline">Fusion = put the two maps one behind the other, then mix.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>class ConvFuser(nn.Sequential):
  def __init__(self, in_channels,
               out_channels):
    self.in_channels = in_channels
    self.out_channels = out_channels
    super().__init__(
      nn.Conv2d(sum(in_channels),
        out_channels, 3, padding=1,
        bias=False),
      nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
      nn.ReLU(True),
    )

  def forward(self, inputs):
    return super().forward(
      torch.cat(inputs, dim=1))</pre><figcaption>fusers/conv.py · the full class</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>fuser:
  type: ConvFuser
  in_channels: [80, 256]
  out_channels: 256</pre><figcaption>convfuser.yaml · the recipe</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c3-5"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.5</span><h3>Find the objects: the head</h3><span class="slides">heads/bbox/transfusion.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-5"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-5" data-got="c3-5"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The <b>head</b> is the last part. Its name is TransFusionHead. It operates like this:</p>
<ol class="steps"><li>It makes a <b>heatmap</b> for each of the 10 object types. A hot square means "an object is probably here".</li><li>It keeps only the hottest square of each small area.</li><li>It takes the 200 best squares. Each one is a <b>proposal</b>.</li><li>A small attention network looks at the map around each proposal.</li><li>It gives the box: center, height, size, direction and speed.</li></ol><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the code</span><p>Line 237 makes the heatmap. Line 266 keeps the local maximum. Lines 270 to 272 take the best proposals.</p></div><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p>You always get 200 boxes, also if the street is empty. Look at the score. A low score means that the model is not sure. When you draw, use <code>--bbox-score 0.3</code> to remove the weak ones.</p></div><div class="box links"><span class="tag">Connects to</span><ul><li><a href="#c6-6">6.6</a> draw the boxes</li><li><a href="#c7-1">7.1</a> change the number of proposals</li></ul></div><p class="oneline">Heatmap → 200 best squares → 200 boxes with scores.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>dense_heatmap = self.heatmap_head(lidar_feat)
...
heatmap = heatmap * (heatmap == local_max)
...
top_proposals = heatmap.view(
    batch_size, -1
).argsort(dim=-1, descending=True)[
    ..., : self.num_proposals
]</pre><figcaption>transfusion.py:237, 266, 270</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>object_classes:
  - car
  - truck
  - construction_vehicle
  - bus
  - trailer
  - barrier
  - motorcycle
  - bicycle
  - pedestrian
  - traffic_cone</pre><figcaption>configs/nuscenes/default.yaml · 10 types</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c3-6"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">3.6</span><h3>The second task: color the road</h3><span class="slides">heads/segm/vanilla.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c3-6"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c3-6" data-got="c3-6"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The map from above can do a second task. The program colors each square: road, crossing, walkway, stop line, parking area, divider. This is <b>BEV map segmentation</b>.</p>
<p>You use the same two sides and the same fusion. You change only the head and some settings. Thus the paper says "multi-task".</p>
<div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>For this task the camera is better than the LiDAR. A line on the road has color but no height. The laser almost does not see it.</p></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">Files that you have</span><p>In <code>pretrained/</code>, names with <code>det</code> find objects. Names with <code>seg</code> color the road.</p></div><p class="oneline">Same map, other head: color the road.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="shot" tabindex="0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Road from above in colors"><figcaption>Demo video · colored road</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>bevfusion-det.pth

</div><div class="quiz" id="quiz3"><div class="quiz-h"><h3>Checkpoint 3: The full model</h3><span class="score"></span></div><div class="q" data-a="b"><p>The camera map has a car at the wrong distance. The scores are low.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q14"> <span>0</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q14"> <span>10</span></label><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q14"> <span>200</span></label><p class="why2">It always gives 200 proposals. The scores are low.</p></div></div><div class="q" data-a="a"><p>Which file joins the two maps?</p><div class="opts jsonly"><button type="button" data-k="a">fusers/conv.py</button><button type="button" data-k="b">backbones/second.py</button><button type="button" data-k="c">vtransforms/lss.py</button></div><p class="why" hidden>ConvFuser is in fusers/conv.py.</p><div class="nojs nq"><label class="r"><input type="radio" name="q15"> <span>fusers/conv.py</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q15"> <span>backbones/second.py</span></label><label class="w"><input type="radio" name="q15"> <span>vtransforms/lss.py</span></label><p class="why2">ConvFuser is in fusers/conv.py.</p></div></div></div></section>
<section class="chapter wrap" id="ch4"><div class="ch-head"><span class="plate">4</span><div><p class="eyebrow">Chapter 4 · Reading code</p><h2>The code</h2></div></div><div class="story"><span class="tag">The story so far</span><p>The project has 22,438 lines of Python. You do not need to read all of them.</p><p>You need a map of the folders. Then you always know where to look.</p></div><div class="goals"><b>After this chapter you can</b><ul><li>Find the file of each station.</li><li>Tell which recipe file has priority.</li><li>Follow one training step in the code.</li></ul></div><div class="cards"><article class="card" id="c4-1"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">4.1</span><h3>The folders</h3><span class="slides">The project folder</span><label class="got" for="got-c4-1"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c4-1" data-got="c4-1"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Folder or file</th><th>Function</th></tr><tr><td><code>configs/</code></td><td>The recipes. A recipe tells the program which parts to use. <b>You change these files most frequently.</b></td></tr><tr><td><code>tools/</code></td><td>The programs that you start: <code>train.py</code>, <code>test.py</code>, <code>create_data.py</code>, <code>visualize.py</code>.</td></tr><tr><td><code>mmdet3d/datasets/</code></td><td>Reads the photos, the points and the correct answers from the disk.</td></tr><tr><td><code>mmdet3d/models/</code></td><td>The stations of chapter 3.</td></tr><tr><td><code>mmdet3d/ops/</code></td><td>Fast code for the graphics card. Most of it is C++ and CUDA.</td></tr><tr><td><code>mmdet3d/core/</code></td><td>Helper code for boxes, points and voxels.</td></tr><tr><td><code>mmdet3d/apis/</code>, <code>runner/</code></td><td>The training loop.</td></tr><tr><td><code>pretrained/</code></td><td>Checkpoints that the authors trained. You already have 7 files.</td></tr><tr><td><code>data/</code></td><td>The dataset. You do not have this folder yet.</td></tr><tr><td><code>runs/</code></td><td>The results of your training. The program makes this folder.</td></tr></table></div><p>The project also has code for <b>radar</b>, a third sensor. You do not use a radar model here.</p><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>Think of a restaurant. <code>configs/</code> = the recipes. <code>tools/</code> = the chefs. <code>models/</code> = the machines. <code>data/</code> = the food. <code>runs/</code> = the plates that come out.</p></div><p class="oneline">Recipes in configs, programs in tools, stations in models.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>bevfusion/
├── configs/      recipes
├── tools/        programs
├── mmdet3d/
│   ├── datasets/ read the data
│   ├── models/   the stations

│   ├── core/     helpers

├── pretrained/   checkpoints

<article class="card solo" id="c4-2"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">4.2</span><h3>The file of each station</h3><span class="slides">mmdet3d/models/</span><label class="got" for="got-c4-2"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c4-2" data-got="c4-2"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Station</th><th>File in <code>mmdet3d/models/</code></th></tr><tr><td>The full model</td><td><code>fusion_models/bevfusion.py</code> <b>(read this file first)</b></td></tr><tr><td><span class="cc">Photo to map</span></td><td><code>vtransforms/base.py</code>, <code>lss.py</code>, <code>depth_lss.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="cc">Join photo features</span></td><td><code>necks/generalized_lss.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="ll">LiDAR network</span></td><td><code>backbones/sparse_encoder.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="mm">Put maps together</span></td><td><code>fusers/conv.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="mm">Look at a larger area</span></td><td><code>backbones/second.py</code>, <code>necks/second.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="mm">Find objects</span></td><td><code>heads/bbox/transfusion.py</code>, <code>centerpoint.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><span class="mm">Color the road map</span></td><td><code>heads/segm/vanilla.py</code></td></tr></table></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">Where to start</span><p>Read in this sequence: <code>fusers/conv.py</code> (22 lines), then <code>forward_single</code> in <code>bevfusion.py</code>, then <code>_bev_pool</code> in <code>base.py</code>.</p></div><p class="oneline">Start with bevfusion.py. It calls all the other files.</p></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c4-3"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">4.3</span><h3>The recipes</h3><span class="slides">configs/</span><label class="got" for="got-c4-3"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c4-3" data-got="c4-3"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>A recipe is a text file. Its name ends with <code>.yaml</code>. Each line has a name and a value.</p>
<p>The program reads more than one file. It starts in the top folder. It reads each <code>default.yaml</code> on the path. Then it reads your file.</p>
<div class="box key need"><span class="tag">Key idea<span class="needtag">Remember this</span></span><p><mark class="need">If two files give different values, the last value is used. Values on the command line have priority over all files.</mark></p></div><figure class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 600 246" role="img" aria-label="The program reads five files in sequence and the last file has priority">
<rect class="bx" x="4" y="6" width="420" height="36" rx="5"/><rect class="bx" x="34" y="54" width="420" height="36" rx="5"/><rect class="bx" x="64" y="102" width="420" height="36" rx="5"/><rect class="bx" x="94" y="150" width="420" height="36" rx="5"/><rect class="bx green" x="124" y="198" width="440" height="40" rx="5"/>
<text x="16" y="29">configs/default.yaml</text><text x="46" y="77">nuscenes/default.yaml</text><text x="76" y="125">det/default.yaml</text><text x="106" y="173">transfusion/… (3 more default files)</text><text class="b" x="136" y="223">lidar/voxelnet.yaml (read last, has priority)</text></svg><figcaption>From general to special. The file at the bottom has priority.</figcaption></figure><div class="box trap"><span class="tag">Trap</span><p>The command line rule is different in <code>test.py</code>. There you write <code>--cfg-options name=value</code>. In <code>train.py</code> and <code>visualize.py</code> you write <code>--name value</code>.</p></div><div class="box analogy"><span class="tag">Analogy</span><p>A family recipe for bread is general. Your grandmother writes a note on it. You write a second note. The last note is the one that you follow.</p></div><p class="oneline">Many small files, the last one has priority.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre># size of one box, in meters
voxel_size: [0.1, 0.1, 0.2]

# passes through the examples
max_epochs: 20

optimizer:
  # how large each change is
  lr: 1.0e-4</pre><figcaption>Example lines of a recipe</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre># file and all default files
configs.load(args.config,
             recursive=True)
# then the command line
configs.update(opts)</pre><figcaption>tools/train.py:28-29 · reading</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c4-4"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">4.4</span><h3>From a name to a class</h3><span class="slides">models/builder.py</span><label class="got" for="got-c4-4"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c4-4" data-got="c4-4"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose">
<p>The recipe uses names, for example <code>type: ConvFuser</code>. The code has a class with the same name. The line <code>@FUSERS.register_module()</code> puts the class into a list. Then the program can find it by its name.</p>
<p>To find a class yourself, search for the name:</p>
<div class="cmd"><div class="cmd-h"><span>Terminal</span><button type="button" class="copy">Copy</button></div><pre>grep -rn &quot;class ConvFuser&quot; mmdet3d</pre></div><div class="box key"><span class="tag">Key idea</span><p>This is why you can change the model without Python code. Change the name in the recipe, and the program uses another class.</p></div><div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>Name in the recipe</th><th>File</th></tr><tr><td><code>BEVFusion</code></td><td><code>fusion_models/bevfusion.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>ConvFuser</code></td><td><code>fusers/conv.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>SparseEncoder</code></td><td><code>backbones/sparse_encoder.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>DepthLSSTransform</code></td><td><code>vtransforms/depth_lss.py</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>TransFusionHead</code></td><td><code>heads/bbox/transfusion.py</code></td></tr></table></div><p class="oneline">The name in the recipe = the name of a class in the code.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>@FUSERS.register_module()
class ConvFuser(nn.Sequential):</pre><figcaption>fusers/conv.py:11-12</figcaption></figure><figure class="codeshot"><pre>FUSIONMODELS = Registry(&quot;fusion_models&quot;)
VTRANSFORMS = Registry(&quot;vtransforms&quot;)
FUSERS = Registry(&quot;fusers&quot;)</pre><figcaption>models/builder.py · three lists</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
<article class="card" id="c4-5"><header class="card-h"><span class="cid">4.5</span><h3>One training step in the code</h3><span class="slides">bevfusion.py · forward_single</span><label class="got" for="got-c4-5"><input type="checkbox" id="got-c4-5" data-got="c4-5"> Got it</label></header><div class="card-b"><div class="prose"><ol class="steps"><li><code>tools/train.py</code> reads the recipe and makes the model.</li><li>The dataset reads one example: 6 photos, the LiDAR points, and the correct boxes.</li><li>The program changes the example a little (card 2.5).</li><li><code>forward_single</code> sends the example through all stations.</li><li>The head compares its boxes with the correct boxes and calculates the loss.</li><li>The computer changes the parameters to decrease the loss.</li><li>After each epoch, the program saves a checkpoint and does a test.</li></ol><div class="box key"><span class="tag">See it in the code</span><p>The code at the right side is the full project in a few lines. Read it three times. First, find "camera" and "lidar". Then find <code>fuser</code>. Then find <code>head.loss</code>.</p></div><div class="box between"><span class="tag">Between the lines</span><p>Open the file and look at lines 297 to 299. In training the sequence of the sensors is normal. In a test it is reversed, and line 329 turns it back. The authors write "avoid OOM". OOM means "out of memory".</p></div><p class="oneline">forward_single: make the maps, join them, find objects, calculate the loss.</p></div><div class="shots"><figure class="codeshot"><pre>for sensor in self.encoders:
  if sensor == &quot;camera&quot;:
    feature = \
      self.extract_camera_features(...)
  elif sensor == &quot;lidar&quot;:
    feature = self.extract_features(
                points, sensor)
  features.append(feature)

if self.fuser is not None:
  x = self.fuser(features)

batch_size = x.shape[0]
x = self.decoder[&quot;backbone&quot;](x)
x = self.decoder[&quot;neck&quot;](x)

pred_dict = head(x, metas)
losses = head.loss(gt_bboxes_3d,
    gt_labels_3d, pred_dict)</pre><figcaption>bevfusion.py:297-347 · shortened</figcaption></figure></div></div></article>
</div><div class="quiz" id="quiz4"><div class="quiz-h"><h3>Checkpoint 4: The code</h3><span class="score"></span></div><div class="q" data-a="b"><p>You want to change the size of a voxel.
